hed: A Quiet Morning on the Desk
deck: Table Rock and Taneycomo, written like a fishing magazine — two waters, one week, nothing invented on the outdoor desk.

play.title: Harvest the spots.
play.body: MDC's Table Rock advice: keep spotted bass. The largemouth and smallmouth will thank you. Put slot rainbows back.

season.name: Dog days
season.why: This is the hard season on the White River system, and it is also when the fishermen who live here quietly catch fish. Thermocline is set. Shad are deep. Table Rock surface is in the 80s. Taneycomo is still 50-degree tailwater.
tips: Fish the first 45 minutes like it matters. After that, put the topwater away.
Table Rock: 15–35 feet, electronics on. You are looking for bait, not banks.
Taneycomo: two- to six-pound test, pink Power Worm, no hero hookset.
MDC wants spotted bass harvested on Table Rock. Keep the spots. Put the 12-to-20-inch rainbows back.
Noon in August is not a fishing hour. Night on the points is a different lake.
License 16–64, plus a trout permit for Taneycomo. Bass Pro at the Landing sells both.

body: ## Hooked on Branson Low, clear water on Table Rock and the predictable Taneycomo generation rhythm (minimal overnight/morning, ramping to 1–4 units mid-afternoon through dark) set up a classic early-fall trout bite. Newly stocked rainbows have migrated up-lake and are aggressive on a wide range of presentations.

Today's Play: Drift or wade during the lower-flow morning window with 1/16–1/8 oz jigs (brown, black, white, sculpin/ginger) or pink worms under a float. Switch to heavier rigs when generation kicks in after lunch. Check the schedule before stepping in.

## The Week No prior dated daily files were present in data/fishing for the last 7 days (directory returned zero matches on modified-order search). Recent patterns from Lilley's Landing (9/17 report) and John Sappington (early September) show Table Rock holding 2–3 ft below pool with low overnight flows and stronger afternoon/evening generation (up to ~13k cfs peaks in late August reports). Water clarity excellent; oxygen lower in the tailwater this time of year. Carry-forward honestly: expect similar low-to-moderate flows most mornings with afternoon pushes. Verify live today.

## In Season Early Fall Transition. Cooling air temperatures (highs near 90s, lows 70s) have trout more active throughout the day rather than just extremes. Stocking continues (recent wave of smaller rainbows moving upstream). Low-oxygen flows from Table Rock still influence tactics. Water temps in the tailwater hold in the mid-50s. Focus on seams, current breaks, and structure as fish fatten for winter.

taneycomo.dek: Cold tailwater · generation is the whole game

now.temp: Tailwater cold (typically ~50–54°F below the dam). Verify at the bank.
now.generation: ~20 cfs at 08:00 CT (USACE live). Call SWPA 866-494-1993 before you wad.

body: This tailwater remains a trophy trout fishery with cold releases from Table Rock keeping it productive year-round. Current water temperature ~56.8°F at School of the Ozarks gauge with DO around 4.5 mg/L. Generation is the tactic book: low or no flow overnight/early morning (prime wading and light-line drifting), then stronger current (1–4 units) from mid-afternoon into dark. Newly stocked smaller rainbows are aggressive and less wary — easy targets on spinners, spoons, jigs, flies, or bait under floats.

Wade below the dam (stay outside the 760-ft closed zone) during low periods with indicator rigs or micro jigs. Drift boats or dock anglers do well when water is moving — use weighted rigs and stay in seams. Slot limit in upper sections (rainbows 12–20" protected; artificials only in trophy area). Below US 65 bridge, trout permit required to possess. Black jigs excel after dark. Pink worms, zebra midges, scuds, and jerkbaits all producing per recent local reports. Water clarity excellent — clean presentations win. Call 866-494-1993 for the latest SWPA schedule.
(Sources: Lilley's 9/17, USGS 07053600 gauge 9/17, John Sappington, Greenough's Guide.)

## Why open this tomorrow Overnight weather (chance of showers, cooling trend) and any shift in SWPA generation (demand-driven) can change wading windows and fish activity fast. A strong rain event upstream or schedule change could alter clarity, oxygen, or flows by morning. Check the gage and schedule again — the bite often improves as we slide deeper into fall.
